clue.text: How you may shortly sign yourself and the rest

definitions.text: How you may shortly sign yourself
definitions.meaning: first meaning: letters to a newspaper editor traditionally close 'Yours, etc.', the phrase in its short form
second meaning: the Latin phrase used to stand for further unlisted items

explanation.walkthrough: Letters to The Times were printed signed off 'Yours etc.', so 'shortly' points to the abbreviation etc. that a writer adds after Yours.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase literally means 'and other things', used to cover further similar items not listed.

clue.text: March hares up to this distance can be heard

indicators.note: March hares are proverbially mad, and a mad word is one whose letters run wild
hares that are up have been stirred and scattered, so their letters are disturbed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Boxing hares in spring are close enough that you can hear them.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'mad as a March hare' lets 'March' signal a jumble while reading as a month.
explanation.definitionFit: Earshot is the range within which sounds are audible, so something within it is near enough to hear.

clue.text: Tory to see about 18 ac's insulting language

indicators.note: about means going around, so the first two pieces enclose the cross-referenced word

parts.note: CON is the abbreviation for Conservative
18 across is a stomach, and a tum is the informal word for it
Ely is a cathedral city and a bishop's see

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician goes to look into somebody's abusive remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is a bishop's diocese; ELY, the Cambridgeshire cathedral city, is the crossword's favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Contumely is an old literary word for scornful, insolent treatment or abusive speech.

clue.text: Rope over width of ship is for keeping rafters together

parts.note: to rope something is to tie it
a ship's beam is its breadth at the widest point

explanation.surface: Sailing talk about a line stretched across a vessel's breadth.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie-beam is the horizontal timber joining the feet of a pair of roof rafters so they cannot spread apart.

clue.text: Blame Shylock's wife for upsetting the Italian painter

parts.note: to take the rap is to take the blame

indicators.note: to upset is to turn over, and in a down clue that sends a word bottom to top

parts.note: Leah is the wife Shylock mentions in The Merchant of Venice

explanation.surface: Someone faults the moneylender's wife for distressing a Renaissance artist.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock recalls the ring his late wife Leah gave him; the name is the only mention of her in the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Raphael was the High Renaissance painter from Urbino, famed for his Madonnas and the Vatican frescoes.

clue.text: Makes up late news items

definitions.meaning: first meaning: invents or falsifies, as figures are dodged
second meaning: stop-press items inserted into a newspaper at the last moment

explanation.walkthrough: A fudge is the newspaper term for a space or column kept for last-minute news; the surface suggests a journalist inventing stories.
explanation.definitionFit: To fudge is to fake or contrive, and the printers' noun names late stop-press insertions in a paper.

clue.text: One who gets a kick from a boot perhaps

definitions.text: One who gets a kick from a boot perhaps

parts.words: One who gets a kick from a boot perhaps
parts.note: surface reading: someone kicked by a footballer or an angry person's shoe
setter's reading: gets a thrill, as from an object of sexual fixation such as footwear

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets a kick' means 'gets pleasure', and boots are a classic object of erotic obsession.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person draws sexual excitement from an object, with shoes and boots the commonest examples.

clue.text: Small car registered in GP's name

indicators.note: something registered in a place is entered inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a GP is a general practitioner, a doctor or doc
the Mini is the classic small British car

explanation.surface: A little car is registered under the family doctor's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominic is a man's given name, so it is an example of the general word.

clue.text: Terminal from defective meter

parts.note: ex is Latin for out of, as in ex-works

indicators.note: a defective item is faulty and out of order, so these letters need rearranging

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A reading comes off a faulty gauge.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe what lies at the very end or furthest limit, as in the terminal or extreme point.

clue.text: Cattle disease about to return in skin plague

indicators.note: in places the preceding piece inside the words that follow

parts.note: rind is the tough outer skin of fruit or cheese

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: re means concerning or about
pest is an old word for plague, as in pestilence

explanation.surface: A livestock illness is set to come back as a plague of the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Rinderpest, German for cattle plague, is a viral disease of cattle declared eradicated in 2011.

clue.text: Marry fellow worker

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to pair up or wed

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like an office romance, but the two words are separate senses: a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To mate is to pair as partners, and a mate is a colleague or assistant on the job.

clue.text: Servant's keen to cook oversize joint

parts.note: a housemaid is a female domestic servant

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A domestic is eager to roast a huge cut of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a roast in a kitchen scene, but it is the body's joint.
explanation.definitionFit: Housemaid's knee is bursitis, a swelling over the kneecap from long kneeling, so the knee joint is enlarged.

clue.text: Air current that makes spring warm

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a rising column of warm air used by gliders and birds
second meaning: the adjective for a naturally heated spring

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' reads as the season but is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names an upward air current, and the adjective describes hot springs heated from underground.

clue.text: A share to delve into

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a portion allotted to someone
second meaning: a rented garden plot that is dug

explanation.walkthrough: 'Delve' is an old word for dig; a British allotment is a small plot of council land rented for growing vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: An allotment is an apportioned amount, and also a garden plot one digs.

clue.text: Dodger from Brooklyn, perhaps, in jug

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a baseball player who throws, as on the Brooklyn Dodgers team
second meaning: a large jug for pouring

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodger' and 'jug' suggest a crook in prison, as jug is slang for jail; the Dodgers were Brooklyn's baseball team.
explanation.definitionFit: A baseball pitcher delivers the ball to batters, and a pitcher is also a vessel with a lip and handle.

clue.text: The courage to settle down in the middle of the country

parts.note: heart is courage, as in take heart
to land is to come down and settle

explanation.surface: Someone finds the nerve to make a home in the interior.
explanation.definitionFit: A heartland is the central or core region of a country, away from coasts and borders.

clue.text: Smart term for a stand-offish type

parts.note: fly is British slang for sharp or knowing
a half is a school term at some British schools

explanation.surface: A clever word for an aloof, unfriendly person.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the fly-half is also called the stand-off half, so 'stand-offish' is a pun, not aloofness.
explanation.definitionFit: The rugby position also known as stand-off links the scrum-half with the three-quarters.

clue.text: Girl with dictionary is roped in

parts.note: a lass is a girl, especially in the North and Scotland
OED is the Oxford English Dictionary

explanation.surface: A young woman carrying a reference book gets drawn into a project.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassoed means caught with a rope noose, which is literally being roped in.

clue.text: Poisonous plant causing fowl pest

parts.note: a hen is a domestic fowl
a bane is a curse or source of ruin

explanation.surface: A toxic weed that harms chickens.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant's name really does come from its supposed effect on poultry.
explanation.definitionFit: Henbane is a foul-smelling nightshade whose leaves and seeds contain toxic alkaloids.

clue.text: Bear a breadbasket

definitions.meaning: first meaning: tolerate or put up with
second meaning: slang for the belly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear a breadbasket' reads as carrying one; breadbasket is old slang for the belly.
explanation.definitionFit: To stomach something is to tolerate it, and the noun names the digestive organ where food goes.

clue.text: Beginners gouge round the shellfish

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the second word wraps around the first

parts.note: to gouge out is to scoop
L stands for a learner driver, so two beginners give two of them

explanation.walkthrough: Learner drivers in Britain carry L-plates, so a beginner is L, and plural beginners two Ls.
explanation.definitionFit: Scollop is an older variant spelling of the fan-shelled bivalve better known as a scallop.

clue.text: Supervise poem in Old English

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: OE is the standard abbreviation for Old English
verse is poetry, a poem

explanation.surface: Someone oversees a poem written in Anglo-Saxon.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversee is to watch over and direct work or people, a direct synonym of supervise.

clue.text: Rustic dance beginning

parts.note: the hay is an old country dance with interweaving figures
a seed is the start or origin of something

explanation.surface: A country dance is getting under way.
explanation.definitionFit: Hayseed is informal, chiefly American, for a country bumpkin, an unsophisticated rural person.

clue.text: Directed to adjudicate about witches being banished

parts.note: directed somewhere is sent there
taken as written
a coven is a gathering of witches
to try a case is to adjudicate it

explanation.surface: Someone was sent to judge on witches who were then exiled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is loose here: the coven comes before the trial. To send someone to Coventry is the British idiom for refusing to speak to them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means ostracised, deliberately shunned and excluded from company, as if exiled.

clue.text: Radio tape containing 50 per cent tittle-tattle

indicators.note: the phrase holds the letters within it, ready to be found across a word boundary

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A broadcast recording full of gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of tittle-tattle is tittle, a tiny jot; the surface reads it as gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: A tittle is a tiny dot or particle, so like the Greek letter it means the smallest amount.

clue.text: One of those current affairs they talk about in the North at tea-time

definitions.text: One of those current affairs they talk about in the North at tea-time

parts.note: surface reading: the news topics people discuss

parts.words: One of those current affairs they talk about in the North at tea-time
parts.note: setter's reading: a currant-filled pastry from a Lancashire town, eaten with afternoon tea

explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' stands for currant, as the word sounds in a northern accent, so the affair is a fruit-filled cake; Eccles is a town near Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: The pastry is a flaky round case of buttery puff filled with currants, named after the Lancashire town.

clue.text: Refer to public notice

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the formal verb ... to, to mention

explanation.walkthrough: The verb is used with 'to', so 'Refer to' as a whole matches it.
explanation.definitionFit: To advert to something is to turn attention or allude to it, and the noun is an announcement promoting something.

clue.text: Article completed without pages being tacked on

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the first words wrap around the last

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
pp is the abbreviation for pages
completed means finished

explanation.surface: A piece of writing was finished with no pages attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Appended means added at the end as a supplement, the same as attached or tacked on.
